name: Liam Farah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm doing economics, and a normal week is four lectures, a stats workshop, and a lot of time in my room on Orchard Lane building things with AI tools. I use them every day: to explain concepts, to test my essay arguments, and to run little data projects. I also write a small newsletter about student money that has about 300 readers. My parents, who run an import business, cover my rent and fees, so I'm not stressed about money.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What are you hoping to get from the degree?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Honestly, a base. I like understanding how economies work, and I want to work somewhere between policy and tech. My school results were average, so I'm not the obvious top candidate, but I learn tools faster than most people I know, and that's my edge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's fine, and I'd keep using the tools anyway because they already save me hours. I'd tell my friends the hype was too much, but it's still useful for the boring bits. I'd probably write a newsletter issue called something like the great AI hangover.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means my edge shrinks a bit, because if everyone's using the tools in a limited way, being fast with them matters less. But it's also safe, and I'd still be a decent economics graduate. I'd worry more about whether average grades get me past the first filter on applications.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the newsletter going and try to double the readers by spring. I'd apply to a summer internship at a think tank or a bank's analytics team. And I'd learn some proper statistics, not just prompts, so that my skills don't depend on one tool.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Less excitement than the other scenarios, but also less pressure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the newsletter make money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not yet, and I don't want it to be a business exactly. But a sponsor asked me about a post last month, which was funny. If it paid even 100 pounds a month I'd be happy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with that money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably put half into a savings account and spend half on a better laptop. My dad says to save all of it, and he's usually right.

feel: **Calm**, with less excitement than the other worlds but also less pressure.

steps.text: Keep the student money newsletter going and double readers
Learn proper statistics so my skills don't depend on one tool
Save half of any newsletter income in a savings account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the people who learn the tools now will have a huge advantage, but also that we need public support for those who can't. I'd write a newsletter issue explaining which entry-level tasks are going first. I'd say unions and governments should set a floor under people while it all shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'm in a decent position because I already work with these tools every day. But I'm not naive: a lot of economics graduate jobs are research, writing and checking, which is exactly what AI takes first. Fewer junior roles means more competition, and my grades are average.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd build a portfolio of real projects: data analysis, short reports, a model of student housing costs. I'd apply for internships a year earlier than normal. And I'd try to turn the newsletter into something that shows my work to employers, maybe with interviews with economists.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited and a little nervous. It feels like a race, and I like races, but I know not everyone does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned public support. What does that look like for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A basic income or a training guarantee, something that doesn't make people beg for help. I think it's fair that the people who gain from the tools pay for a safety net.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you see a conflict between that and being someone who benefits from AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. I'm lucky I'm fast with tools, and my parents can pay for me. That's why I think someone like me should push for rules, not just ride the wave.

I'd say governments should set a **floor** under people while it all shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the biggest thing happening to the economy in my lifetime and nobody is ready. I'd write about it constantly. I'd say it needs emergency rules, a basic income, and maybe a public stake in the big AI systems.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my degree might not matter. Thinking work done better and cheaper by 2028 means economists, analysts and researchers are first in line. I'd be 20, second year, and the tools I'm good at are the ones that replace me. That's an odd feeling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop treating the degree as the point and treat it as a place to build contacts. I'd get into policy groups pushing for a basic income and retraining. And I'd work out what hands-on skill might last till 2031, maybe through my dad's warehouse business, where I'd learn logistics from the floor up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, with a rush of adrenaline. I'd be sleeping badly but also oddly motivated.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would you go to your dad's warehouse?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because it's physical, it's real, and it'll be the last part to be automated. And I'd learn how a business actually works, which no lecture teaches.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your parents say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mum would be delighted that I'm interested, and Dad would worry that I'm giving up on a degree. I'm not giving up on my degree, I'm hedging.

I'd push for emergency rules and a **basic** income.

fieldNote: Becomes **anxious** because his own skill, thinking work, is what gets replaced.
Chooses a physical **hedge** in the family warehouse.

steps.text: Join groups campaigning for a basic income and retraining

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a real window, and the question is who uses it. I'd tell friends to learn the tools, build a network and save a bit. I'd write about which jobs look safest in 2031 and which look weakest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel unusually well placed. By 2031 I'd be 23, just out of university, and I'd have spent five years with these tools. That gives me a head start, as long as employers still hire graduates. If they don't, my advantage doesn't help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree, but build income of my own as early as possible. I'd turn the newsletter into a small paid analysis service, probably for student groups first. I'd spread my savings over a few things and keep some cash. And I'd learn some basic coding so I'm closer to the machine, not just a user.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Energised, a bit anxious. I'd rather have five years and be nervous than be surprised.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does spreading savings mean for a student?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much, honestly, maybe 2,000 pounds. But the habit matters. I'd put some in an index fund and keep some in cash, so that if my path breaks, I'm not starting from zero.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if employers stop hiring graduates altogether?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then my plan is to be self-employed with a small client list. It's risky, but I'm the kind of person who'd try it, and my parents would back me for a year or two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years gives us room to get it right, but only if we start now. I'd write about how an economy should share the gains. I'd tell friends it's a good moment to be curious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I feel fine. Ten years is a whole career's first stage. I'd be 28 by 2036, working, and I'd have changed jobs once or twice anyway. It's the people who'd be 55 who should worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree, take a policy-and-tech job, and keep building. I'd keep learning each new tool as it comes, probably one new thing a quarter. I'd also volunteer for the policy side, such as a think tank, because the next ten years of rules will matter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and curious. It's the first one where I feel like a participant, not a target.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want your older relatives to do in that decade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My uncle runs a shop, and I'd tell him to learn the tools early. Not to run the business with AI, just to see what it does, so he's not scared when it arrives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a worry left for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That the gains go to a few firms and the rest of us get a shrug. That's what I'd push on.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one. Two years is too fast for universities, my parents' business, or any government to catch up. What would help is a basic income or training guarantee that's already in place before it hits, plus honest advice from university about which skills last.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I'd like you to ask more people like me whether we feel guilty about being comfortable with this. I do, a bit, and that's why I'd push for support for people who are not.

headlineQuote: I'd be sleeping badly but also oddly motivated.
portrait: Liam is an 18-year-old **economics** student who uses AI tools every day and writes a small newsletter about student money.
His parents run an import business and pay his rent and fees, a **cushion** he says openly.
He is progressive, backing a basic income and rules, yet enthusiastic about tools and early to **learn** them.
He moves from calm to **anxious** in the 2-year world, because thinking work is what he's good at.
biggestWorry: The **2028** world worries him most, because no university, firm or government can catch up in two years.
whatWouldHelp: A basic income or training **guarantee** in place before the change, plus honest advice about which skills last.
